site_id01: Jipijapa, province of Manabi
subpractice_description_raw: SS: Simple-shade agroforests (managed with four to nine tree species, simple vertical structure, tree density regulated to reduce excessive shading and understorey relatively open)
out_exp_design: The three habitat types selected were simple-shade agroforests (managed agroforests with 4–9 shade tree species, simple vertical structure, tree density regulated to reduce excessive shading and understorey relatively open, 8 sites), complex-shade agroforests (managed with 9–12 shade tree species, complex vertical structure with a multi-layered canopy, 8 sites) and abandoned coffee agroforests (abandoned for 10–15 years due to low revenues and currently resembling secondary forests, 14–20 shade tree species, forest regeneration and only few old coffee plants remaining, 6 sites) totaling 22 study sites. We carried out field surveys of spider mites (adults, nymphs, larvae and eggs) and leaf miners (pupae and larvae) in the three types of coffee agroforests at monthly intervals over a whole year (from August 2004 to July 2005). In each study site, we randomly selected 20 coffee plants located at least 5 m away from habitat boundaries and conducted monthly surveys of spider mites and leaf miners. We evaluated 120 coffee leaves per study site (six per plant) in each survey, and averaged the number of spider mites and leaf miners (all developmental stages pooled) on a per-site basis. We randomly chose 10 coffee plants per study site and collected 60 fruits per plant for berry borer survey.  Final numbers were averaged per site, so per treatment, n = no. sites
data_location: Text p. 124

site_id01: Finca Irlanda and Finca Hamburgo, Tapachula, Soconusco
subpractice_description_raw: Forest: a forest fragment
out_exp_design: 4 sampling locations in each of 4 habitat types.  For birds: Four point counts (10 min each) were conducted at each sample location (four per habitat type). Each morning, beginning at dawn, points were sampled, altering direction and starting point to minimize temporal bias (Bibby et al. 1992). AU birds heard and seen within 25 m were noted during each 10-min point count. For butterflies: Two standard butterfly bait traps used at the center of each sampling point, one in the understory (approximately 1 m above the ground) and one in the canopy (hung from a branch of an emergent tree). Traps were set for a period of 8 days within each treatment and were baited with a mash of fermented plantain or banana before each sampling day. Traps were checked on alternate days within the 8-day period for a total of four samples per trap. For ants: Ground-foraging ants were sampled by establishing a 14 X 14 m plot with the random point located at the center of the plot. Tuna ñsh baits (with a volume of approximately 1 cm ) were placed on the ground, forming a 7 X 7 grid system with baits separated by 2 m from each other for a total of 49 baits per plot (Perfecto  and Snelling 1995). Samples of ground-foraging ants were conducted only in three of the four random points per habitat.
data_location: Data extracted from Fig 3a and b using GetData Graph Digitiser. Lat-longs taken from actual farm locations from Google Maps for Tapachula, and from municipality centre from Open Street Maps for Huixtla because Fincas were not registered on any map. This paper estimates total species richness for each taxonomic group using the COMDYN package, which adjusts observed numbers to make comparisons across locations. Details from the paper: One of the biggest challenges of studying and managing tropical diversity is the impossibility of completely surveying all of the species present. As a result, any attempt to compare biodiversity between different locations or among different taxonomic groups confronts the problem that an unknown number of species were left out of every sample, making comparisons of sampled diversity equivocal. Various diversity indices have been created to compensate for this limitation, but all come with their own sets of assumptions and drawbacks (Magurran 1988). For  comparisons of species richness, Nichols et al. (1998) provide an elegant solution in the form of a software package, COMDYN, that uses a bootstrap approach to predict an estimate of total species richness.

site_id01: The field experiment took place at an agricultural research station in Zurich-Reckenholz, Switzerland, from March to July 2009.
subpractice_description_raw: BW: monoculture
out_exp_design: Four replicate blocks, each with six 33 x 1.08 m plots, were sown with Pm3a, Pm3b, and Bobwhite SH 98 26 monocultures and the three 1:1 mixtures Pm3a/Bobwhite, Pm3b/Bobwhite, and Pm3a/ Pm3b. AUDPC was calculated from assessing mildew infection on individual plants at three time points (for 10 individual plants per plot). Seed yield was measured by cutting all (10) individual plants at ground level and seperating vegetative and reproductive parts. The reproductive parts were threshed to obtain seeds and determine total seed mass per plant. N = 4 replicates x 10 plants = 40.
data_location: Biodiversity outcome from figure 1_A; Yield outcome from figure 1_E

out_exp_design: Wildflower plantings at 5 farms. Only four sites were sampled in 2012 (year 4). At each site, the field adjacent to the wildflower planting was paired with a control field of the same cultivar (Duke, Bluecrop, Jersey, or Elliott) adjacent to a regularly mown grassy field margin that was not sown with native seeds, that is, the typical field perimeter. During peak crop bloom, observations were made on 30 blueberry bushes in each of the crop fields adjacent to the wildflower plantings and the control perimeters. Insects visiting blueberry flowers were observed on 15 bushes spaced between 1 and 4 m along the edge of the crop field for 15 min. This was repeated 15 m into the crop interior parallel to the border. Observers walked along the bushes stopping and recording the identity and number of  insects observed visiting blueberry flowers during warm, calm and sunny days between 10:00 and 17:00 h. The abundance of each pollinator group observed visiting blueberry flowers per observation was compared between treatments. Data were analysed separately for each year, pooling the abundance data for observations taken along the crop edge and those taken within the interior for each of the two treatments. Therefore N per year =number of sites per year = 4 for year 4

site_id01: southwest Michigan, USA (details in Supporting Information).
subpractice_description_raw: Control: with a typical perimeter of a drive lane and mown grass at least 9 m wide (mean area = 0.14 ± 0.03 ha), without the addition of sown native wildflowers.
out_exp_design: In 2009, a single wildflower planting was established at each of five highbush blueberry (V. corymbosum L.) farms in southwest Michigan, USA. Additional natural enemy and insect herbivore sampling was conducted with yellow sticky traps deployed for seven days each month from May to September of each year. Each of the crop fields adjacent to wildflower plantings and those adjacent to control perimeters received eight yellow sticky traps: four traps along the crop edge and four 15 m into the interior, placed approximately 1–2 m high within bush canopies. After one week deployed in the field, traps were collected and taken back to the laboratory for evaluation. 8). Data were analyzed separately for each year (natural log + 1 transformation for non-normal data), pooling the abundance data from the crop edge and from the interior for each of the two treatments.  Shannon diversity values were also compared separately for each year. (5 farms x 1 week per month x 5 months = 25)
data_location: Biodiversity outcomes from figure 1 (Year 2011). Vacuum data were not recorded because it was taken from field margins. Yield outcome from table 1 in pdf 1667

site_id01: The experiment took place in 2013 during a single growing season in eight cider apple orchards located in Herefordshire, south-west England (52_x005F_x0001_050–52_x005F_x0001_120 N and 2_x005F_x0001_470– 2_x005F_x0001_560 W).
subpractice_description_raw: Control: apple orchard with grass strip control (alleyways under normal management)
out_exp_design: The experiment took place in 2013 during a single growing season in eight cider apple orchards located in Herefordshire. 4 orchards were planted with flower strips and 4 were not (controls) (from Supplementary Table S1). Plots in orchards were marked out at 0, 50, 100, 150 (so 4 plots per orchard), and in the four largest orchards (3 of which have flower strips, 1 which is control), 200 m (so 5 plots per orchard) from an adjacent area of semi-natural habitat. So in total, for the control there were 1 orchard with 5 plots + 3 orchards with 4 plots = 17 plots; for the flower strip treatment there were 3 orchards with 5 plots and 1 with 4 plots = 19 plots.Yield sampling unit: Developing flower buds were counted on five branches in each plot approximately two weeks before tree blossom. N yield = 17 in control, 19 in flower strip treatment.  Biodiversity sampling unit: During this period (June–August 2012), insect visitation to flower strips in orchards was recorded on six separate occasions using similar methods (walked transects) to those described for observations of insect visitors to apple flowers in 2013. Observations of insect visitation took place in May 2013 during peak bloom in orchards. A single observation consisted of continuously walking alongside trees of a plot for ten minutes. During this period, all insects observed visiting apple flowers were recorded. Each plot was observed three to five times over the study period. Visits were analysed as visit rates per plot (number of visits per observation divided by number of apple flowers).  N for apple flower visits in control treatments = 17 plots x median 4 observation occasions = 68; N in flower strip treatments = 19 plots x 4 observations = 76.
data_location: Yield outcomes from figure 3 (final). Biodiversity outcomes from figure 2 (apple flower visits in 2013)

site_id01: Sao Tome
subpractice_description_raw: Tropical forest, possibly including some secondary forest on abandoned agricultural lands
out_exp_design: We defined 28 transects in shade plantations and 20 in forest. These transects were distributed across the island to capture both natural and anthropogenic variability (Fig. S1). Each transect consisted of five points, separated by between 200 and 250 m (240 points in total). Bird assemblages were sampled during the dry seasons (from the middle of May until the end of August) of 2009 and 2010, with at least two weeks separating counts in the same transect. To make sure that there was no observer bias between point-counts, each sampling point was surveyed three times. We counted the number of individuals of all species that were detected visually or aurally during 10-min point-counts. We used first order jackknife to estimate endemic and non-endemic species richness in forest and in shade plantation for both taxa, and sample-based rarefaction curves to evaluate differences in species richness between land uses. These techniques allow comparing species richness of land-use types with different sample sizes.
data_location: Data from Table 3. Lat-long is centroid of all sites (individiual site locations could be digitised from Supplementary info if needed later)

site_id01: Northeast Colombia
subpractice_description_raw: Cloud forest fragment (CFF): historically have been used for selective small-scale wood extraction by local farmers.
out_exp_design: We established a total of 13 linear transects with a length of 60m subdivided in three 20m subunits (SU) as smallest possible sample unit, on which faunal data acquisition was based. Transects are oriented parallel to respective contour lines and distributed across the matrix according to the respective land-use systems and altitudinal gradients following a stratified random design. This resulted in the establishment of two transects on CP (1200–1350m a.s.l.), three in NSP (1280–1350m a.s.l.), four in SP (1300–1450m a.s.l.), two in CFF (1400–1470m a.s.l.), and two in WL (1130 and 1340m a.s.l).
data_location: Data from Fig3a,b,c using WebPlotDigitiser. Lat-long is centroid of study area (only info provided)

out_exp_design: We established a total of 13 linear transects with a length of 60m subdivided in three 20m subunits (SU) as smallest possible sample unit, on which faunal data acquisition was based. Transects are oriented parallel to respective contour lines and distributed across the matrix according to the respective land-use systems and altitudinal gradients following a stratified random design. This resulted in the establishment of two transects on CP (1200–1350m a.s.l.), three in NSP (1280–1350m a.s.l.), four in SP (1300–1450m a.s.l.), two in CFF (1400–1470m a.s.l.), and two in WL (1130 and 1340m a.s.l).

site_id01: Oxfordshire
subpractice_description_raw: Standard margin (tussocky sown perennial grass strips) with or without hedgerow trees
out_exp_design: 48 samples at 3 sites in each of 4 farms x 4 years for each treatment (standard margin, extended margin etc).  Macro-moths were sampled during four consecutive years (2006– 2009; 240 trap nights; 1920 trap events) using light traps with 48 fixed sampling sites. Data from all sampling periods and sites within each farm were combined to get an overall abundance and richness measure per year and this is what was used to extract median and CI values in this database. Therefore we record the sample size N = 16, i.e. number of farms per treatment x 4 years.
data_location: Data from Fig. 2 using WebPlot. Lat-long is centroid of all sites. Individual sites available from Fig 1a but unnamed so cannot be matched to data

out_exp_design: The total number of fields studied was 48, with 15 (ten cereals and five mixed) in organic farms, 16 in conventional mixed farms and 17 in conventional cereal farms. Carabid beetles were collected using pitfall traps (mouth diameter 70 mm, volume 170 ml, half-filled with 70% ethylene glycol and a few drops of detergent) in three two-week sampling periods during the first half of June, July and August, respectively. In each of the 48 studied fields, a nine-trap transect (traps 5 m apart) was placed starting 1 m from the field margin towards the centre of the field. Carabids were identified to species level using identification keys by Lindroth (1985, 1986). For statistical analysis the carabid data from the three sampling periods were pooled.

site_id01: the Langfang Experimental Station of Plant Protection Institute, CAAS, Hebei Province
subpractice_description_raw: Control: wheat monoculture
out_exp_design: Three replicates per treatment with five 1m plot. The number of S. avenae apterae was observed in five 1 m2 plots that were chosen uniformly in each plot. Within each sampling plot, thirty randomly selected wheat tillers were used as one sampling unit. Sitobion avenae alatae was sampled using yellow sticky traps (30 × 20 cm) (Zhu and Park 2005; Wang et al. 2009), which were individually fixed on bamboo poles at 1.2 m above the ground in the center of each plot. Each yellow sticky trap was replaced by a new trap after each counting. Lady beetles at all stages on all wheat plants within the “1 m2 plot” squares, which covered three rows of wheat, were counted and identified in the center of each plot. Aphid parasitoids were collected by 20 sweeps of an insect net of 30 cm in diameter and 50 cm in length in three rows at the center of each plot and identified under a dissecting microscope in the laboratory. Insects were sampled in the field every 5 days from April 12 to June 6 in 2008, and from April 12 to May 27 in 2009.
data_location: Fig. 1 A (year 2009). Yield from Table 2 My LER values are much higher than in the paper (see Table 2). Not clear why, but retained mine for transparency in calculation.

site_id01: the Kenya Agricultural Research Institute (KARI) Regional Research Centre at Mtwapa, Coast Province, Kenya
subpractice_description_raw: Maize monocrop: maize planted alone
out_exp_design: Randomised block design with five replicates, where the study covered 6 cropping seasons (so yield N = 6 x 5). Three species of stem-borers were encountered at Mtwapa; Sesamia calamistis, C. partel- lus and Chilo orichalcociliellus. Dispensers were loaded with the synthetic pheromone between 1400 and 1500 hours and mounted on sticky Phercon I C traps which were placed 50 cm above the ground, one at the center of each plot between 1600 and 1800 hours the same day (Lux et al., 1994). Adult moths were collected and counted twice weekly (Wednesday and Sunday) for a period of one year (December 1993 to November 1994). Fresh pheromone was loaded onto the traps during each moth collection day. Data about the total number of male moths were analysed. Abundance per plot (5 plots per treatment)
data_location: Figure 1

site_id01: Hawaii's Agricultural Research Stations on the island of Oahu at Waimanalo
subpractice_description_raw: Bareground: zucchini monoculture
out_exp_design: Herbivorous insects and predators were sampled by randomly selecting five plants from the inner rows excluding border plants and all alatae and apterous aphids were counted. During the first sampling period four whole leaves, two fully expanded older leaves and two median expanded leaves were sampled by gently turning each leaf and counting all alatae and apterous aphids, thrips, adult white¯ies and all predators encountered. After the first sampling period an `eight leaf sampling unit' was used. This consisted of exam- ining four fully expanded older leaves and four median expanded leaves. Because of high insect numbers, subsamples were used; one-half of the leaf as denoted by the midrib vein was examined and all counts were converted into number per leaf. (First period 4 leaves per plant x 5 plants per plot x 2 plots=40) (Second period 8 leaves per plant x 5 plants per plot x 2 plots= 80)
data_location: Yield data from Table 1 (plant biomass taken instead of yield data from Fig 3, because yield data does not include variance), Arthropods figure 1 B Waimanalo

out_exp_design: Nine leaves were randomly sampled at three leaf positions (upper, middle and lower), three leaves in each position, within one soybean plant. The number of insect pest species was counted on each leaf. The whole plant as a sampling unit was investigated for natural enemies. A diagonal systematic sampling scheme was used in this experiment (Subramani 2000), and 25 plants were chosen at random in each plot. Insect surveys were performed at seven-day intervals, beginning at 32 days after planting. site_id01: the Lincoln University Horti- cultural Research Area, Lincoln, Canterbury
subpractice_description_raw: Control: a flower-free control where the main crop grew. (broccolli or lucerne)
out_exp_design: In this study, we examine the influence of single and multiple species flower treatment patches on three key beneficial insects in two agroecosystems (broccoli and lucerne) over a 5-week period. The number of insects of each species that were present inside a randomly positioned 1-m2 quadrat was recorded every minute for 15 min using a scan sampling method with instantaneous recording (Martin & Bateson, 1993). Only the minute with the highest number of species were used in the analysis. Plots sampled once weekly for 5 weeks. 2 replicates of broccolli, 2 replicates of lucerne. Therefore N=5x4=20
data_location: Figure 1.

site_id01: Jipijapa, province of Manabi
subpractice_description_raw: CS: complex-shade agroforests (managed with 9–12 tree species, complex vertical structure)
out_exp_design: The three habitat types selected were simple-shade agroforests (managed agroforests with 4–9 shade tree species, simple vertical structure, tree density regulated to reduce excessive shading and understorey relatively open, 8 sites), complex-shade agroforests (managed with 9–12 shade tree species, complex vertical structure with a multi-layered canopy, 8 sites) and abandoned coffee agroforests (abandoned for 10–15 years due to low revenues and currently resembling secondary forests, 14–20 shade tree species, forest regeneration and only few old coffee plants remaining, 6 sites) totaling 22 study sites. We carried out field surveys of spider mites (adults, nymphs, larvae and eggs) and leaf miners (pupae and larvae) in the three types of coffee agroforests at monthly intervals over a whole year (from August 2004 to July 2005). In each study site, we randomly selected 20 coffee plants located at least 5 m away from habitat boundaries and conducted monthly surveys of spider mites and leaf miners. We evaluated 120 coffee leaves per study site (six per plant) in each survey, and averaged the number of spider mites and leaf miners (all developmental stages pooled) on a per-site basis. We randomly chose 10 coffee plants per study site and collected 60 fruits per plant for berry borer survey.  Final numbers were averaged per site, so per treatment, n = no. sites
data_location: Text p. 124

As a result, any attempt to compare biodiversity between different locations or among different taxonomic groups confronts the problem that an unknown number of species were left out of every sample, making comparisons of sampled diversity equivocal. Various diversity indices have been created to compensate for this limitation, but all come with their own sets of assumptions and drawbacks (Magurran 1988). For  comparisons of species richness, Nichols et al. (1998) provide an elegant solution in the form of a software package, COMDYN, that uses a bootstrap approach to predict an estimate of total species richness.

site_id01: Sanxing Town, Chongming District, China
subpractice_description_raw: Multispecies co-culture plots: Taro and the two ornamental flower species were transplanted in the three cauliflower-aquatic animal co-culture blocks in 2013 and 2014 in the following manner: Taro (conventional varieties from Chongming local  farmers)was interplanted with spring maize (Zea mays) in late April. In middle-to-late September, the maize was harvested, but taro plants were left intact. In late August, cauliflower was interplanted into the plots with taro. In the 22 plots in each co-culture block, 7 plots were planted with taro. Plots taro were spaced with 2-plot intervals. In the plots with both cauliflower and taros, two rows of taro and five rows of cauliflower were interplanted with 0.6 m between neighbouring cauliflower and/or taro. Cosmos was planted along one side of the water-filled ditch and balsamin was planted along the other two parallel sides of the ditches from late June to early July each year. The interrow distance of cosmos or balsamin was 0.2e0.3 m.
out_exp_design: the six samplings for herbivores and predators (at 20 points in each block) were carried out from early September to early-to-middle November at appropriately 10-15-days intervals, in 2013 and again in 2014. Here, we use only the 2014 data.  22 plots x 3 blocks per control/treatment = 66 plots of monoculture, 66 plots of co-culture. Number of samples at each time point = 20 x 3 blocks = 60.
data_location: Figure 3 A (2014). Yield and amount of pesticide from Figure 5 B and D. Yield sampling strategy not explained and so assumed to match the sampling strategy used for biodiversity data collection, i.e. same N. Only cauliflower yields provided

site_id01: southwest Michigan, USA (details in Supporting Information).
subpractice_description_raw: Flower A perennial wildflower seed mix (Michigan Wildflower Farm, Portland, MI) was selected that consisted of 15 species of Michigan native wildflowers with bloom periods that together span May through October and have been shown to be attractive to bees (Tuell et al. 2008).
out_exp_design: Wildflower plantings at 5 farms. Only four sites were sampled in 2012 (year 4). At each site, the field adjacent to the wildflower planting was paired with a control field of the same cultivar (Duke, Bluecrop, Jersey, or Elliott) adjacent to a regularly mown grassy field margin that was not sown with native seeds, that is, the typical field perimeter. During peak crop bloom, observations were made on 30 blueberry bushes in each of the crop fields adjacent to the wildflower plantings and the control perimeters. Insects visiting blueberry flowers were observed on 15 bushes spaced between 1 and 4 m along the edge of the crop field for 15 min. This was repeated 15 m into the crop interior parallel to the border. Observers walked along the bushes stopping and recording the identity and number of  insects observed visiting blueberry flowers during warm, calm and sunny days between 10:00 and 17:00 h. The abundance of each pollinator group observed visiting blueberry flowers per observation was compared between treatments. Data were analysed separately for each year, pooling the abundance data for observations taken along the crop edge and those taken within the interior for each of the two treatments. Therefore N per year =number of sites per year = 4 for year 4

site_id01: The experiment took place in 2013 during a single growing season in eight cider apple orchards located in Herefordshire, south-west England (52_x005F_x0001_050–52_x005F_x0001_120 N and 2_x005F_x0001_470– 2_x005F_x0001_560 W).
subpractice_description_raw: Flower strip: orchards were sown with targeted flower mixtures of up to 25 wildflower species in April 2011
out_exp_design: The experiment took place in 2013 during a single growing season in eight cider apple orchards located in Herefordshire. 4 orchards were planted with flower strips and 4 were not (controls) (from Supplementary Table S1). Plots in orchards were marked out at 0, 50, 100, 150 (so 4 plots per orchard), and in the four largest orchards (3 of which have flower strips, 1 which is control), 200 m (so 5 plots per orchard) from an adjacent area of semi-natural habitat. So in total, for the control there were 1 orchard with 5 plots + 3 orchards with 4 plots = 17 plots; for the flower strip treatment there were 3 orchards with 5 plots and 1 with 4 plots = 19 plots.Yield sampling unit: Developing flower buds were counted on five branches in each plot approximately two weeks before tree blossom. N yield = 17 in control, 19 in flower strip treatment.  Biodiversity sampling unit: During this period (June–August 2012), insect visitation to flower strips in orchards was recorded on six separate occasions using similar methods (walked transects) to those described for observations of insect visitors to apple flowers in 2013. Observations of insect visitation took place in May 2013 during peak bloom in orchards. A single observation consisted of continuously walking alongside trees of a plot for ten minutes. During this period, all insects observed visiting apple flowers were recorded. Each plot was observed three to five times over the study period. Visits were analysed as visit rates per plot (number of visits per observation divided by number of apple flowers).  N for apple flower visits in control treatments = 17 plots x median 4 observation occasions = 68; N in flower strip treatments = 19 plots x 4 observations = 76.
data_location: Yield outcomes from figure 3 (final). Biodiversity outcomes from figure 2 (apple flower visits in 2013)

subpractice_description_raw: Hedgerow: plantings approximately 7 m wide were estab-lished at our study sites in 1996–2003 and were comprised ofa row of native perennial shrubs, 305–550 m long, bordered bynative perennial grasses. Plant species composition for each sitevaried somewhat but all contained California buckwheat (Erio-gonum fasciculatum foliolosum), California lilac (Ceanothus griseus),California coffeeberry (Rhamnus californica tomentella), coyotebrush (Baccharis pilularis), elderberry (Sambucus mexicana), andtoyon (Heteromeles arbutifolia). Three-meter wide strips of native perennial grasses wereplanted along one or both sides of the hedgerow to help sup-press weeds and create overwintering habitat for natural enemies;species included purple needlegrass (Nassella pulchra), noddingneedlegrass (N. cernua), California onion grass (Melica californica),one-sided bluegrass (Poa secunda), blue wildrye (Elymus glaucus),and creeping wildrye (Leymus triticoides). In some sites how-ever, few grasses remained, having been outcompeted by weeds.The primary herbaceous weeds occurring in hedgerows weremustard (Brassica spp.), field bindweed (Convolvulus arvensis), mal-low (Malva parviflora and neglecta), and bristly oxtongue (Picrisechioides), and varied among sites.

site_id01: Maine
subpractice_description_raw: PR:Pollination Reservoirs in lowbush blueberry. three different PRs:clover, wildflower, and natural regeneration. NR: natural regeneration. blueberry field with adjacent natural habitat. Natural regeneration treatments were not seeded; all plants emerged from the existing seed bank. For a list of sown species and seeding rates, see Tables 1 and 2. We selected plant species by first compiling a literature-based list of the flowering plants known to attract pollinators (Stubbs et al. 1992, Stubbs and Coverstone 2004, Tuell et al. 2008, Mader et al. 2011). Invasive species were removed, keeping only those that were either native or naturalized in Maine. WILDFLOWER: Oats were hand broadcast as a nurse crop in the wildflower treatment only. Planting dates ranged from 8 June to 20 June 2012. During seedling establishment, plots were watered as needed.
out_exp_design: All PR treatment sites (n=3) were paired with a control (n=3), which consisted of a nearby (1.5–20 km), similarly managed lowbush blueberry field without PR treatments. In the 2012, 2013, and 2015 growing seasons, we measured the influence of PRs on wild bee pollination services. At all sites with paired PR and control fields (n=6), we measured fruit set and visitation rates to blueberry flowers.
data_location: Biodiversity outcome from figure 3. Yield outcome from figure 4 (2015). Variance assumed to be SE, based on values reported in Table 4

site_type01: A management practice often used in southern Brazil is the fallow cycle, where the land is allowed to rest for 1–3 years after harvest. Before 1980, most of the rice fields were managed with fallow periods between 4 and 6 years, and extensive livestock was an alternative economic support to farmers. However, the need for larger crops to sustain the market led to a large decrease in the amount of fallow time.
site_id01: Capivari do Sul, Rio Grande do Sul
subpractice_description_raw: Crops with fallow SP: The three rice fields with fallow experienced the same resting period as the land (2 years without rice cultivation), which was used by livestock during this time. During the fallow period, the fields could have small intermittent ponds after rainfall.
out_exp_design: 3 fields in each treatment, sampled 5 times through the year_x000D_
data_location: Sampling effort: 40minutes x 2 nights x 5 times x 3 fields = 12 hrs. Data extracted from Fig 2 using WebPot Digitalizer

site_id01: Sao Tome
subpractice_description_raw: Shade plantations, where 80% of selected plantations had cocoa, 25% had coffee, 10% had both cocoa and coffee, and 5% had only other crops such as banana and taro
out_exp_design: We defined 28 transects in shade plantations and 20 in forest. These transects were distributed across the island to capture both natural and anthropogenic variability (Fig. S1). Each transect consisted of five points, separated by between 200 and 250 m (240 points in total). Bird assemblages were sampled during the dry seasons (from the middle of May until the end of August) of 2009 and 2010, with at least two weeks separating counts in the same transect. To make sure that there was no observer bias between point-counts, each sampling point was surveyed three times. We counted the number of individuals of all species that were detected visually or aurally during 10-min point-counts. We used first order jackknife to estimate endemic and non-endemic species richness in forest and in shade plantation for both taxa, and sample-based rarefaction curves to evaluate differences in species richness between land uses. These techniques allow comparing species richness of land-use types with different sample sizes.
data_location: Data from Table 3. Lat-long is centroid of all sites (individiual site locations could be digitised from Supplementary info if needed later)

subpractice_description_raw: Shaded plantation (SP): Shaded cocoa and coffee plantations with mixed shade trees
out_exp_design: We established a total of 13 linear transects with a length of 60m subdivided in three 20m subunits (SU) as smallest possible sample unit, on which faunal data acquisition was based. Transects are oriented parallel to respective contour lines and distributed across the matrix according to the respective land-use systems and altitudinal gradients following a stratified random design. site_id01: Oxfordshire
subpractice_description_raw: Extended (6m) margin (tussocky sown perennial grass strips) with or without hedgerow trees
out_exp_design: 40 samples at 3 sites in each of 4 farms x 4 years for each treatment (standard margin, extended margin etc).  Macro-moths were sampled during four consecutive years (2006– 2009; 240 trap nights; 1920 trap events) using light traps with 40 fixed sampling sites. Data from all sampling periods, sites and years within each farm were combined to get an overall abundance and richness measure and this is what was used to extract median and CI values in this database. Therefore we record the sample size N = 4, i.e. number of farms per treatment.
data_location: Data from Fig. 2 using WebPlot. Lat-long is centroid of all sites. Individual sites available from Fig 1a but unnamed so cannot be matched to data

subpractice_description_raw: Maize: Alley cropping with poplar
out_exp_design: 10.5 x 10.0 m x 6 replicates
product_raw: Araneae (spiders), the parasitic wasp superfamily Chalcidoidea (Hymenoptera) and the beetle family Carabidae (Coleoptera)

out_exp_design: The total number of fields studied was 48, with 15 (ten cereals and five mixed) in organic farms, 16 in conventional mixed farms and 17 in conventional cereal farms. Carabid beetles were collected using pitfall traps (mouth diameter 70 mm, volume 170 ml, half-filled with 70% ethylene glycol and a few drops of detergent) in three two-week sampling periods during the first half of June, July and August, respectively. In each of the 48 studied fields, a nine-trap transect (traps 5 m apart) was placed starting 1 m from the field margin towards the centre of the field. Carabids were identified to species level using identification keys by Lindroth (1985, 1986). For statistical analysis the carabid data from the three sampling periods were pooled.

site_id01: the Langfang Experimental Station of Plant Protection Institute, CAAS, Hebei Province
subpractice_description_raw: 2-2 mixtures of wheat and pea rows (each ratio represent- ing the ratio of the number of rows of wheat to that of the rows of pea)
out_exp_design: Three replicates per treatment with five 1m plot. The number of S. avenae apterae was observed in five 1 m2 plots that were chosen uniformly in each plot. Within each sampling plot, thirty randomly selected wheat tillers were used as one sampling unit. Sitobion avenae alatae was sampled using yellow sticky traps (30 × 20 cm) (Zhu and Park 2005; Wang et al. 2009), which were individually fixed on bamboo poles at 1.2 m above the ground in the center of each plot. Each yellow sticky trap was replaced by a new trap after each counting. Lady beetles at all stages on all wheat plants within the “1 m2 plot” squares, which covered three rows of wheat, were counted and identified in the center of each plot. Aphid parasitoids were collected by 20 sweeps of an insect net of 30 cm in diameter and 50 cm in length in three rows at the center of each plot and identified under a dissecting microscope in the laboratory. Insects were sampled in the field every 5 days from April 12 to June 6 in 2008, and from April 12 to May 27 in 2009.
data_location: Fig. 1 A (year 2009). Yield from Table 2 My LER values are much higher than in the paper (see Table 2). Not clear why, but retained mine for transparency in calculation.

subpractice_description_raw: PU: highly disturbed rainforest fragments.  which also contained portions of abandoned coffee or cardamom plantations with a mixed canopy of native rainforest trees and planted exotic trees such as Maesopsis emenii and Spathodea campanulata (Muth- uramkumar et al. 2006; Mudappa and Raman, in press).
out_exp_design: The area covered by each transect varied and hence, for each transect, the number of spiders detected on each transect was divided by the area of the transect and multiplied by 100 to obtain spider species density per 100 m2. Five belt transects were surveyed in each fragment at least once every month between January and May 2005, except in the largest site (IYAK) where seven transects were surveyed, and in MA and AN where four transects were surveyed. site_id01: Field experiments were carried out at two locations 13.5 km apart in the Limpopo Province of South Africa, on a smallholder farmers field at Dalmada.
subpractice_description_raw: 2: maize + lablab two plants m-1 length

data_location: Table 2 (Dalmada with lablab planted at 84d or, simultaneously with maize) Only maize yields provided. Unclear if lablab is harvested but it is often used for food so we classify this as intercropping.

site_id01: the Kenya Agricultural Research Institute (KARI) Regional Research Centre at Mtwapa, Coast Province, Kenya
subpractice_description_raw: Intercrop 1.5 m: maize were planted between leucaena hedgerows planted 1.5 m apart
out_exp_design: Randomised block design with five replicates, where the study covered 6 cropping seasons (so yield N = 6 x 5). Three species of stem-borers were encountered at Mtwapa; Sesamia calamistis, C. partel- lus and Chilo orichalcociliellus. Dispensers were loaded with the synthetic pheromone between 1400 and 1500 hours and mounted on sticky Phercon I C traps which were placed 50 cm above the ground, one at the center of each plot between 1600 and 1800 hours the same day (Lux et al., 1994). Adult moths were collected and counted twice weekly (Wednesday and Sunday) for a period of one year (December 1993 to November 1994). Fresh pheromone was loaded onto the traps during each moth collection day. Data about the total number of male moths were analysed. Abundance per plot (5 plots per treatment)
data_location: Figure 1

site_id01: Hawaii's Agricultural Research Stations on the island of Oahu at Waimanalo
subpractice_description_raw: Buckwheat: zucchini + buckwheat
out_exp_design: Herbivorous insects and predators were sampled by randomly selecting five plants from the inner rows excluding border plants and all alatae and apterous aphids were counted. During the first sampling period four whole leaves, two fully expanded older leaves and two median expanded leaves were sampled by gently turning each leaf and counting all alatae and apterous aphids, thrips, adult white¯ies and all predators encountered. After the first sampling period an `eight leaf sampling unit' was used. This consisted of exam- ining four fully expanded older leaves and four median expanded leaves. Because of high insect numbers, subsamples were used; one-half of the leaf as denoted by the midrib vein was examined and all counts were converted into number per leaf. (First period 4 leaves per plant x 5 plants per plot x 2 plots=40) (Second period 8 leaves per plant x 5 plants per plot x 2 plots= 80)
data_location: Yield data from Table 1 (plant biomass taken instead of yield data from Fig 3, because yield data does not include variance), Arthropods figure 1 B Waimanalo

subpractice_description_raw: Yellow mustard: zucchini + yellow mustard
out_exp_design: Arthropods on zucchini foliage were sampled by randomly select- ing ten plants from the interior rows, excluding border plants, and all alatae and apterous aphids, adult white- ¯ies and all generalist predators were counted. During the first sampling period a `four leaf sampling unit' was used. This consisted of looking at two fully expanded older leaves and two median expanded leaves of ten plants. Because of the high number of aphids encountered during the remaining sampling period a `two leaf sampling unit' was used which consisted of looking at one fully expanded older intact leaf and one median expanded leaf. (First period: 4 leaves per plant x 10  plants per plot x  2 plot per treatment= 80) (Second period= 2 leaf per plant x 10 plants per plot x 2 plots per treatment= 40)
data_location: Yield data from Fig 7 (only grade A+Jumbo), Arthropods figure 4 B Poamoho

site_id01: The experiments were conducted at the teaching and research station of China Agricultural University in Hebei Province (lat.
subpractice_description_raw: MC: in which the seeds of the five cultivars above were mixed evenly (by weight) before planting.
out_exp_design: Nine leaves were randomly sampled at three leaf positions (upper, middle and lower), three leaves in each position, within one soybean plant. The number of insect pest species was counted on each leaf. The whole plant as a sampling unit was investigated for natural enemies. A diagonal systematic sampling scheme was used in this experiment (Subramani 2000), and 25 plants were chosen at random in each plot. Insect surveys were performed at seven-day intervals, beginning at 32 days after planting. (for insect pest sample unit = 9 leaves x 25 plants x 4 plots replication =900) (for natural enemies sample unit = 25 plants x 4 plots replication=100)
data_location: Tabla 2 (2011). Vegetative grown

site_id01: Yolo County, an intensively-farmed agricultural region of California’s Central Valley
subpractice_description_raw: Hedgerows: sunflowers fields halfwere adjacent to hedgerows (hedgerows contained more plant species and more blooms than control weedy edges)
out_exp_design: We established two 200m transects within each field, perpendicular to the field edge or hedgerow and 100m apart (Fig. S1b). We netted and observed pollinators at four distances along these transects: 10, 50, 100 and 200m from the edge. We varied the starting sampling location within fields and edges at each study site (surveyors started at different starting distances on each transect) to reduce conflation of distance with temporal variation in bee foraging behavior, which peaks in the morning and late afternoon (Pisanty et al., 2014). The mean is given by field ( 5 control/hedgerows sunflower fields in 2012 + 4 control/hedgerows sulflower fields in 2013 = 9 sunflower fields per treatment)
data_location: Second paragraph of results (Aerial netting; HEADGEROWS AND CONTROL IN THE FIELD). In the supplementary data they give the specific location of the fields

site_id01: Bonga, Ethiopia
subpractice_description_raw: shaded coffee home gardens
out_exp_design: A quadrat (various sizes depending on taxa) in each 1km2 site, including 13 sites for plantation, 15 for forest, 14 for home gardens
data_location: Figure 2. Coordinates are for the centroid of the area. Sites are located at max 30km. The home gardens of the southwestern Ethiopian highlands could be classified as an agroforestry system even though the density of trees is relatively low compared with many shaded coffee or cacao farm systems described from other parts of the world (e.g., Perfecto et al. 1996; Bos et al. 2007; L´opez-G´omez et al. 2008). The overall number of tree species in the home garden system over a landscape can, however, be relatively high (Abebe 2005).

site_id01: southwest Michigan, USA (details in Supporting Information).
subpractice_description_raw: Control: regularly mown grassy field margin that was not sown with native seeds,
out_exp_design: Wildflower plantings at 5 farms. Only four sites were sampled in 2012 (year 4). At each site, the field adjacent to the wildflower planting was paired with a control field of the same cultivar (Duke, Bluecrop, Jersey, or Elliott) adjacent to a regularly mown grassy field margin that was not sown with native seeds, that is, the typical field perimeter. During peak crop bloom, observations were made on 30 blueberry bushes in each of the crop fields adjacent to the wildflower plantings and the control perimeters. Insects visiting blueberry flowers were observed on 15 bushes spaced between 1 and 4 m along the edge of the crop field for 15 min. This was repeated 15 m into the crop interior parallel to the border. Observers walked along the bushes stopping and recording the identity and number of  insects observed visiting blueberry flowers during warm, calm and sunny days between 10:00 and 17:00 h. The abundance of each pollinator group observed visiting blueberry flowers per observation was compared between treatments. Data were analysed separately for each year, pooling the abundance data for observations taken along the crop edge and those taken within the interior for each of the two treatments. Therefore N per year =number of sites per year = 4 for year 4

site_id01: The experiment took place in 2013 during a single growing season in eight cider apple orchards located in Herefordshire, south-west England (52_x005F_x0001_050–52_x005F_x0001_120 N and 2_x005F_x0001_470– 2_x005F_x0001_560 W).
subpractice_description_raw: Control: apple orchard with grass strip control (alleyways under normal management)
out_exp_design: The experiment took place in 2013 during a single growing season in eight cider apple orchards located in Herefordshire. 4 orchards were planted with flower strips and 4 were not (controls) (from Supplementary Table S1). Plots in orchards were marked out at 0, 50, 100, 150 (so 4 plots per orchard), and in the four largest orchards (3 of which have flower strips, 1 which is control), 200 m (so 5 plots per orchard) from an adjacent area of semi-natural habitat. So in total, for the control there were 1 orchard with 5 plots + 3 orchards with 4 plots = 17 plots; for the flower strip treatment there were 3 orchards with 5 plots and 1 with 4 plots = 19 plots.Yield sampling unit: Developing flower buds were counted on five branches in each plot approximately two weeks before tree blossom. N yield = 17 in control, 19 in flower strip treatment.  Biodiversity sampling unit: During this period (June–August 2012), insect visitation to flower strips in orchards was recorded on six separate occasions using similar methods (walked transects) to those described for observations of insect visitors to apple flowers in 2013. Observations of insect visitation took place in May 2013 during peak bloom in orchards. A single observation consisted of continuously walking alongside trees of a plot for ten minutes. During this period, all insects observed visiting apple flowers were recorded. Each plot was observed three to five times over the study period. Visits were analysed as visit rates per plot (number of visits per observation divided by number of apple flowers).  N for apple flower visits in control treatments = 17 plots x median 4 observation occasions = 68; N in flower strip treatments = 19 plots x 4 observations = 76.
data_location: Yield outcomes from figure 3 (final). Biodiversity outcomes from figure 2 (apple flower visits in 2013)

site_id01: the Kenya Agricultural Research Institute (KARI) Regional Research Centre at Mtwapa, Coast Province, Kenya
subpractice_description_raw: Maize monocrop: maize planted alone
out_exp_design: Randomised block design with five replicates, where the study covered 6 cropping seasons (so yield N = 6 x 5). Three species of stem-borers were encountered at Mtwapa; Sesamia calamistis, C. partel- lus and Chilo orichalcociliellus. Dispensers were loaded with the synthetic pheromone between 1400 and 1500 hours and mounted on sticky Phercon I C traps which were placed 50 cm above the ground, one at the center of each plot between 1600 and 1800 hours the same day (Lux et al., 1994). Adult moths were collected and counted twice weekly (Wednesday and Sunday) for a period of one year (December 1993 to November 1994). Fresh pheromone was loaded onto the traps during each moth collection day. Data about the total number of male moths were analysed. Abundance per plot (5 plots per treatment)
data_location: Figure 1

site_id01: Hawaii's Agricultural Research Stations on the island of Oahu at Waimanalo
subpractice_description_raw: Bareground: zucchini monoculture
out_exp_design: Herbivorous insects and predators were sampled by randomly selecting five plants from the inner rows excluding border plants and all alatae and apterous aphids were counted. During the first sampling period four whole leaves, two fully expanded older leaves and two median expanded leaves were sampled by gently turning each leaf and counting all alatae and apterous aphids, thrips, adult white¯ies and all predators encountered. After the first sampling period an `eight leaf sampling unit' was used. This consisted of exam- ining four fully expanded older leaves and four median expanded leaves. Because of high insect numbers, subsamples were used; one-half of the leaf as denoted by the midrib vein was examined and all counts were converted into number per leaf. (First period 4 leaves per plant x 5 plants per plot x 2 plots=40) (Second period 8 leaves per plant x 5 plants per plot x 2 plots= 80)
data_location: Yield data from Table 1 (plant biomass taken instead of yield data from Fig 3, because yield data does not include variance), Arthropods figure 1 B Waimanalo

subpractice_description_raw: Multispecies co-culture plots: Taro and the two ornamental flower species were transplanted in the three cauliflower-aquatic animal co-culture blocks in 2013 and 2014 in the following manner: Taro (conventional varieties from Chongming local  farmers)was interplanted with spring maize (Zea mays) in late April. In middle-to-late September, the maize was harvested, but taro plants were left intact. In late August, cauliflower was interplanted into the plots with taro. In the 22 plots in each co-culture block, 7 plots were planted with taro. Plots taro were spaced with 2-plot intervals. In the plots with both cauliflower and taros, two rows of taro and five rows of cauliflower were interplanted with 0.6 m between neighbouring cauliflower and/or taro. Cosmos was planted along one side of the water-filled ditch and balsamin was planted along the other two parallel sides of the ditches from late June to early July each year. The interrow distance of cosmos or balsamin was 0.2e0.3 m.
out_exp_design: the six samplings for herbivores and predators (at 20 points in each block) were carried out from early September to early-to-middle November at appropriately 10-15-days intervals, in 2013 and again in 2014. Here, we use only the 2014 data.  22 plots x 3 blocks per control/treatment = 66 plots of monoculture, 66 plots of co-culture. Number of samples at each time point = 20 x 3 blocks = 60.
data_location: Figure 3 A (2014). Yield and amount of pesticide from Figure 5 B and D. Yield sampling strategy not explained and so assumed to match the sampling strategy used for biodiversity data collection, i.e. same N. Only cauliflower yields provided

out_exp_design: Wildflower plantings at 5 farms. Only four sites were sampled in 2012 (year 4). At each site, the field adjacent to the wildflower planting was paired with a control field of the same cultivar (Duke, Bluecrop, Jersey, or Elliott) adjacent to a regularly mown grassy field margin that was not sown with native seeds, that is, the typical field perimeter. During peak crop bloom, observations were made on 30 blueberry bushes in each of the crop fields adjacent to the wildflower plantings and the control perimeters. Insects visiting blueberry flowers were observed on 15 bushes spaced between 1 and 4 m along the edge of the crop field for 15 min. This was repeated 15 m into the crop interior parallel to the border. Observers walked along the bushes stopping and recording the identity and number of  insects observed visiting blueberry flowers during warm, calm and sunny days between 10:00 and 17:00 h. The abundance of each pollinator group observed visiting blueberry flowers per observation was compared between treatments. Data were analysed separately for each year, pooling the abundance data for observations taken along the crop edge and those taken within the interior for each of the two treatments. Therefore N per year =number of sites per year = 4 for year 4

subpractice_description_raw: 2-2 mixtures of wheat and pea rows (each ratio represent- ing the ratio of the number of rows of wheat to that of the rows of pea)
out_exp_design: Three replicates per treatment with five 1m plot. The number of S. avenae apterae was observed in five 1 m2 plots that were chosen uniformly in each plot. Within each sampling plot, thirty randomly selected wheat tillers were used as one sampling unit. Sitobion avenae alatae was sampled using yellow sticky traps (30 × 20 cm) (Zhu and Park 2005; Wang et al. 2009), which were individually fixed on bamboo poles at 1.2 m above the ground in the center of each plot. Each yellow sticky trap was replaced by a new trap after each counting. Lady beetles at all stages on all wheat plants within the “1 m2 plot” squares, which covered three rows of wheat, were counted and identified in the center of each plot. Aphid parasitoids were collected by 20 sweeps of an insect net of 30 cm in diameter and 50 cm in length in three rows at the center of each plot and identified under a dissecting microscope in the laboratory. Insects were sampled in the field every 5 days from April 12 to June 6 in 2008, and from April 12 to May 27 in 2009.
data_location: Fig. 1 A (year 2009). Yield from Table 2 My LER values are much higher than in the paper (see Table 2). Not clear why, but retained mine for transparency in calculation.

subpractice_description_raw: Intercrop 1.5 m: maize were planted between leucaena hedgerows planted 1.5 m apart
out_exp_design: Randomised block design with five replicates, where the study covered 6 cropping seasons (so yield N = 6 x 5). Three species of stem-borers were encountered at Mtwapa; Sesamia calamistis, C. partel- lus and Chilo orichalcociliellus. Dispensers were loaded with the synthetic pheromone between 1400 and 1500 hours and mounted on sticky Phercon I C traps which were placed 50 cm above the ground, one at the center of each plot between 1600 and 1800 hours the same day (Lux et al., 1994). Adult moths were collected and counted twice weekly (Wednesday and Sunday) for a period of one year (December 1993 to November 1994). Fresh pheromone was loaded onto the traps during each moth collection day. Data about the total number of male moths were analysed. Abundance per plot (5 plots per treatment)
data_location: Figure 1
